experiment.title: CPU vs naive GPU vs tiled GPU

verification.metric: naive GPU: max over n of (max rel. error) / (√n·u)
verification.reference: float64 product of 16 sampled rows at n = 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048

verification.metric: tiled GPU: max over n of (max rel. error) / (√n·u)
verification.reference: float64 product of 16 sampled rows at n = 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048

verification.metric: CPU baseline: max over n of (max rel. error) / (√n·u)
verification.reference: float64 product of 16 sampled rows at n = 64, 128, 256, 512

verification.metric: naive vs tiled: max over n of max |naive − tiled| / |C| / (√n·u)
verification.reference: the two GPU kernels on the same inputs (same summation order: expected 0 without FMA differences)

interpretation.claim: naive GPU: time grows like n³
interpretation.predicted: log-log slope 3 (2n³ flops; ±0.15 for cache effects)
interpretation.note: Fitted over the sizes with n ≥ 512 (n² threads, enough to fill the GPU) whose timed sample (GPU (timestamp) time per product × products per pass) is at least 1 ms (n = 512 … 2048); smaller grids leave the GPU partly idle, so their times do not grow like n³ yet. Over all 6 sizes the slope is 2.08.

interpretation.claim: tiled GPU: time grows like n³
interpretation.predicted: log-log slope 3 (2n³ flops; ±0.15 for cache effects)
interpretation.measured: 3.01 (no interval from 2 points) over n = 1024 … 2048
interpretation.note: Fitted over the sizes with n ≥ 512 (n² threads, enough to fill the GPU) whose timed sample (GPU (timestamp) time per product × products per pass) is at least 1 ms (n = 1024 … 2048); smaller grids leave the GPU partly idle, so their times do not grow like n³ yet. Over all 6 sizes the slope is 2.00. At least 3 sizes are needed for an uncertainty; with fewer, this claim stays undecided (run to n = 2,048).

interpretation.claim: CPU (blocked JS): time grows like n³
interpretation.predicted: log-log slope 3 (2n³ flops; ±0.15 for cache effects)
interpretation.note: Fitted over the sizes whose median time is at least 1 ms (n = 128 … 512), so the timer resolves them. Over all 4 sizes the slope is 2.37.

interpretation.claim: Tiling speeds the GPU kernel up
interpretation.predicted: tiled faster (speedup > 1): 16× fewer global loads (arithmetic intensity 4 vs 0.25 flop/byte); typically 2–10× on real GPUs
interpretation.note: The range is conservative (naive q1 / tiled q3 … naive q3 / tiled q1); undecided when it contains 1. The tiled kernel also reads A and B along rows (coalesced) where the naive one reads A across rows, so part of the gain is access pattern, not only reuse. On a software GPU workgroup memory is ordinary memory and barriers are expensive, so tiling can lose.

interpretation.claim: The naive kernel is bound by memory traffic, not arithmetic
interpretation.predicted: naive GFLOPS ≤ 0.25 × the bandwidth that serves its loads (8 bytes per multiply-add); tiled ≤ 4 × bandwidth
interpretation.measured: naive: 1450 GB/s of loads, tiled: 209 GB/s of global loads, at n = 2048
interpretation.note: Compare with your GPU's memory bandwidth (not known to the page). If the naive figure exceeds it, caches are serving most of its loads: the reuse happens, but in cache rather than in workgroup memory, and cache bandwidth is the limit.

interpretation.claim: The GPU beats one CPU core from some n on
interpretation.predicted: yes: GPU time is ≈ a fixed launch cost until the GPU is full, CPU time grows like n³ from the start (CPU measured up to n = 512)
interpretation.measured: GPU faster from n = 64 on; at n = 512: tiled GPU 0.393 (0.360–0.393) ms vs CPU 110.0 (109.1–110.5) ms
interpretation.note: Kernel time only; with upload and readback the tiled GPU takes 1.550 ms (wall). Where the crossover falls depends on the GPU, the CPU and the browser; undecided when the spreads overlap.

interpretation.claim: Brute-force time vs N (log-log slope, GPU ms)
interpretation.predicted: 2: N − 1 interactions for each of N bodies, O(N²) (± 0.1 for the rest of the fixed cost), fitted above 4× the fixed floor
interpretation.measured: 2.01 (95% CI 1.81 … 2.22, 3 points) over N = 16,384 … 65,536, floor subtracted
interpretation.note: Fitted over the sizes whose median GPU ms is at least 4× the floor (the median at N = 1,024, 66 µs) and at least 1 ms, i.e. ≥ 1.00 ms: N = 16,384 … 65,536; the floor is subtracted before fitting. Smaller sizes are mostly fixed cost, so their time does not grow with the algorithm's work yet. Over all 7 sizes, without the correction, the slope is 1.54.

interpretation.claim: Barnes-Hut time vs N (log-log slope, GPU ms)
interpretation.predicted: about N log N: 1.09 over N = 32,768 … 262,144 (the fitted sizes); accepted 1.00 … 1.29 (the O(N) tree build pulls it to 1, interactions per body growing faster than log N push it up), fitted above 4× the fixed floor
interpretation.measured: 1.18 (95% CI 1.05 … 1.31, 4 points) over N = 32,768 … 262,144, floor subtracted
interpretation.note: Fitted over the sizes whose median GPU ms is at least 4× the floor (the median at N = 1,024, 0.46 ms) and at least 1 ms, i.e. ≥ 1.84 ms: N = 32,768 … 262,144; the floor is subtracted before fitting. Smaller sizes are mostly fixed cost, so their time does not grow with the algorithm's work yet. Over all 9 sizes, without the correction, the slope is 0.87.

interpretation.claim: Barnes-Hut interactions per body vs N (log-log slope)
interpretation.predicted: between 0 and 1: grows, but slower than brute force's N − 1 (→ log N for large N, 0.11 here; CI: 0.37)
interpretation.note: Deterministic counts (one distribution, one seed): the interval reflects curvature, not noise.

interpretation.claim: Crossover N (Barnes-Hut faster from here)
interpretation.predicted: exists: O(N²) overtakes O(N log N) at some N (CI, software GPU, wall ms: between 8,192 and 16,384)
interpretation.measured: between N = 16,384 and N = 32,768 (log-interpolated ≈ 16,400)
interpretation.note: Compared on GPU ms. Device-dependent: compare it with other devices, not with a fixed number. The interquartile ranges do not overlap at either point, so the bracket is resolved.

interpretation.claim: Tree-build share of Barnes-Hut GPU time vs N
interpretation.predicted: falls with N: the build is O(N) plus about 30 fixed dispatches, the traversal O(N log N)

interpretation.claim: Fixed cost per force evaluation (the time at the smallest N)
interpretation.predicted: informational, no verdict: a cost that does not grow with N (submission, synchronisation, and for Barnes-Hut 31 dispatches, 30 of them the tree build); the time at the smallest N bounds it from above
interpretation.measured: Barnes-Hut 0.46 ms at N = 1,024 (GPU ms; ≤ 15 µs per dispatch over 31); brute force 66 µs at N = 1,024 (GPU ms; 1 dispatch)
interpretation.note: The slope fits above use only sizes at least 4× above these (and ≥ 1 ms) and subtract them. At the largest Barnes-Hut N (262,144) the floor is 1% of the time.

interpretation.claim: Crossover: bitonic (global) (GPU timestamps) becomes faster than the CPU sort
interpretation.predicted: device-dependent, no universal N; "none in range" is a valid outcome
interpretation.measured: faster from the smallest N with resolvable times on (bitonic (global) 0.92 ms (0.79–0.98) vs CPU 1.91 ms (1.90–1.91) at N = 131,072); below that N a time is under 10× the timer resolution, so whether the crossover lies lower is undetermined; not compared (a time below 10× the timer resolution): N = 16,384, 32,768, 65,536
interpretation.note: The GPU time is the sort pass alone (no upload or readback): GPU timestamps when the browser has timestamp-query and they are consistent with the wall clock, else submit → done wall time. The CPU sort is wall-clock; each sample is a batch of back-to-back sorts long enough to resolve. A GPU is "faster" at an N only when its q3 is below the CPU sort's q1, and an N is compared only when both medians are at least 10× their clock's resolution (performance.now(): 100 µs, measured; GPU timestamps: 65.5 µs, inferred from the medians). In CI, on a CPU-emulated GPU, there is no crossover. Your GPU, driver, browser and CPU all move this point.

interpretation.claim: Ranking at the largest N (N = 4,194,304, GPU timestamps)
interpretation.predicted: fastest first: radix < bitonic (workgroup memory) < bitonic (global), on a GPU with fast workgroup memory
interpretation.measured: radix 5.83 ms (5.80–5.87) < bitonic (workgroup memory) 13.0 ms (12.9–13.0) < bitonic (global) 25.4 ms (23.3–28.6)
interpretation.note: A prediction for GPUs with fast workgroup memory, not a law: other GPUs and drivers may order them differently. Each adjacent pair counts as decided only when the interquartile ranges are more than one clock tick apart; GPU timestamps are used only when every algorithm's are consistent with the wall clock. On the CPU-emulated GPU in CI the order is inverted (global bitonic fastest, radix slowest): there barriers are expensive and workgroup memory is ordinary cache.
